title: S&P 500, Dow enter correction as AI selloff caps brutal week
dek: US markets are closed for the weekend after Friday's slide left the S&P 500 and Dow more than 10% below their records and wiped out the Nasdaq's gain for 2026. Next week is a holiday-shortened one, with GDP and PCE inflation data landing Wednesday before Thanksgiving.
quick: Weekend edition: no US trading today. Friday's close set the tone: S&P 500 down 3.7%, Nasdaq down 5.3%, Dow down 1.9%, and the VIX fear gauge near 36.
Nvidia fell about 14% Friday, extending its longest weekly losing streak since 2008, after reports that the SEC is examining its accounting.
Anthropic slid about 8.5% in its second day of trading to roughly $89, still above its $83 IPO price.
Treasury yields dropped sharply as investors sought safety, but rate futures still price a Fed hike at the December 8-9 meeting.
Bitcoin traded near $58,000 Saturday morning after dipping below $56,000 overnight; gold sits at its lowest since September 2025.
Next week: markets closed Thursday for Thanksgiving; Wednesday brings Q3 GDP, October PCE inflation and the Fed's Beige Book.

blocks.head: The AI selloff pushes the S&P 500 and Dow into correction
blocks.what: US stocks fell hard on Friday. The S&P 500 lost 3.7% to 6,910.39 and the Dow dropped 1.9% to 48,147.33, leaving both more than 10% below their record closes, the common definition of a correction, according to Reuters and CNBC. The Nasdaq Composite sank 5.3% to 22,617.73, erasing its gain for the year. The VIX volatility index jumped about 26% to near 36.
blocks.why: A correction in both broad indexes signals the selloff has spread beyond a handful of chip stocks. A VIX in the mid-30s means options traders expect large daily swings to continue, which tends to keep pressure on high-valuation growth stocks and support defensive sectors and Treasurys.
blocks.watch: Whether Monday's flash PMI data and Wednesday's inflation report steady sentiment, or whether selling resumes in a thin holiday week.

blocks.head: Nvidia drops 14% as the SEC reportedly examines its accounting
blocks.what: Nvidia shares fell about 14% Friday, reaching their lowest level since June 2025 and extending a weekly losing streak that CNBC and MarketWatch describe as the longest since the 2008 financial crisis. Reuters and The New York Times reported that the SEC is looking into the company's accounting practices; neither Nvidia nor the SEC commented in those reports. The news comes after Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO, with CFO Colette Kress serving as interim chief, and Nvidia's board has said it does not plan to reinstate him.
blocks.why: Nvidia is one of the largest weights in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq, and its chips sit at the center of AI spending plans, so its slide drags on index performance and on chip suppliers worldwide. Other chipmakers fell with it: Micron and AMD each lost roughly 13% to 14% Friday.
blocks.watch: Any formal disclosure from Nvidia about the SEC inquiry, and further board or leadership announcements.

blocks.head: Anthropic gives back part of its record IPO gain
blocks.what: Anthropic, which priced the largest IPO on record at $83 a share, opened Thursday at $111.50 and closed at $97.17. On Friday the stock fell about 8.5% to around $88.91, at one point trading only a few cents above its IPO price, according to The Wall Street Journal and CNBC.
blocks.why: Some investors had hoped a strong debut would mark a turning point for AI stocks; analysts quoted by Reuters said it did not act as that clearing event. How the stock trades relative to its $83 offer price is now being watched as a gauge of appetite for AI risk.

blocks.head: Fed still seen raising rates in December, even as bond yields fall
blocks.what: Rate futures continue to price an interest-rate increase at the Fed's December 8-9 meeting. As of Thursday, CME FedWatch showed about a 91% chance of a quarter-point hike and about 9% for a half-point move. Fed Governor Christopher Waller has said the Fed should consider a half-point hike if it does not clearly signal another increase for January, and Governor Lisa Cook has said further hikes are needed to bring inflation down. Minutes of the October meeting showed nearly all officials expect a quarter-point hike in December.
blocks.why: Higher short-term rates raise borrowing costs and weigh on stock valuations, especially for growth and tech shares. Friday's drop in yields reflected investors buying Treasurys for safety, not a change in Fed expectations, so the stock selloff and hawkish Fed are hitting risk assets at the same time.
blocks.watch: Wednesday's October PCE inflation report, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge.

blocks.head: Trump threatens a 'tremendous tax' on companies building data centers abroad
blocks.what: Speaking at the White House Friday after his trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, President Trump said he would tax US companies that build AI data centers outside the country. He gave no details on the size, legal basis or timing, and said his team was hearing about it for the first time, according to NBC News, The Hill and The New York Times.
blocks.why: Major cloud and AI companies have announced data-center projects overseas, so any such policy could change their spending plans and costs. Analysts note Congress, not the president, holds the authority to impose taxes, so the market impact depends on whether a concrete proposal follows.

blocks.head: CrowdStrike reported in talks to buy Zscaler
blocks.what: Zscaler shares jumped roughly 16% to 18% in after-hours trading Friday after Bloomberg and Reuters reported that CrowdStrike is in talks to acquire the cybersecurity company, which has a market value of about $32 billion. Neither report said a deal had been agreed. CrowdStrike shares fell about 6% to 8% after hours.
blocks.why: A deal would be one of the largest in cybersecurity and could lift other software security names on takeover expectations, while the acquirer's stock typically falls on the cost of a large purchase.
blocks.watch: Confirmation or denial from either company before Monday's open.

blocks.text: Asia

Asian markets had their worst week in years on Friday. Taiwan's main index fell about 6.2%, capping its worst week since 1991, according to Reuters and other outlets. South Korea's KOSPI dropped 5.2% to about 4,870, back below 5,000, and Japan's Nikkei 225 fell about 5.1% to 56,437, with SoftBank Group down by double digits. Losses were smaller in China: the Hang Seng fell 1.9% and Shanghai 1.2%. MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan lost 3.2% on the day and 8.3% on the week, its worst week since March 2020, per Reuters. Chip-heavy markets were hit hardest because their companies supply Nvidia and other AI hardware buyers.
Europe

The Stoxx 600 fell 2.0% to 625.65, its fifth straight decline, leaving it down about 5.8% for the week, its worst week since March. Germany's DAX dropped 2.6% and the UK's FTSE 100 about 1.0%. Chip-linked stocks such as ASML and STMicroelectronics fell more than 9%, according to Reuters. Separately, the UK and EU agreed a deal Friday covering food exports, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme, per the BBC and The Guardian.
Currencies

The yen was the standout safe haven for the week, rising against all major currencies. The dollar weakened about 0.7% against the yen on Friday to around 158.5, moving away from the 160 level that traders watch for possible Japanese intervention. The dollar index ended near 103.8, little changed on the day; CNBC noted it was near a 19-month high earlier Friday on Fed hike expectations. The euro was flat at about $1.097, the pound near $1.308, and the dollar firmed slightly against China's yuan to about 6.68.

US stock and futures markets are closed for the weekend, so the table below reflects Friday's close. Futures finished Friday well below Thursday's levels, matching the cash indexes: Nasdaq 100 futures were down nearly 5% and S&P 500 futures about 3%. The Russell 2000 small-cap index fell 2.8%, a smaller drop than the Nasdaq, as the selling was concentrated in large tech and chip stocks.
With volatility elevated, weekend headlines, including any news on Nvidia, the Zscaler talks or the data-center tax threat, could set the tone when futures reopen Sunday evening at 6 p.m. ET.

Treasury yields fell sharply on Friday as investors moved money from stocks into government bonds. The 2-year yield, which tracks Fed expectations, dropped roughly 11 to 14 basis points to about 4.65%, according to CNBC and other data providers. The 10-year fell about 10 basis points to roughly 4.94%-4.95%, its fifth straight daily decline, and the 30-year slipped about 6 basis points to around 5.32%-5.34%. The curve steepened slightly, with the gap between 2-year and 10-year yields near 30 basis points.

The Fed under Chair Kevin Warsh resumed raising rates in September and held steady in October, when Governor Cook was among the dissenters who favored a hike. Markets broadly expect an increase at the December 8-9 meeting and more next year, according to Reuters. Fed funds futures as of Thursday priced about a 91% chance of a quarter-point hike and 9% of a half-point move, per CME FedWatch.
Fed speakers

items: No Fed officials are scheduled to speak this weekend.
Next week: the Fed's Beige Book survey of regional business conditions is due Wednesday afternoon, ahead of the December meeting's pre-meeting quiet period.

blocks.text: Sectors

Technology was the worst S&P 500 sector Friday, falling about 7.3% as chipmakers sold off. Industrials (down 3.1%), consumer discretionary (down 3.0%) and communication services (down 2.7%) also lagged, reflecting their exposure to AI spending and megacap tech. Consumer staples was the only sector to rise, gaining about 0.7%, while health care was nearly flat and energy and utilities dipped less than 1%. That pattern shows investors rotating into defensive, steady-earnings businesses.
Notable movers

items: Nvidia: down about 14% on reports of an SEC accounting inquiry, following its CEO's departure.
Micron and AMD: each down roughly 13% to 14% in the broad chip selloff.
Anthropic: down about 8.5% to near $89 in its second trading day.
General Mills: up about 5% as investors sought defensive food stocks.
UnitedHealth: up roughly 3% after TD Cowen upgraded it to buy.
Zscaler: up 16% to 18% after hours on reports CrowdStrike is in takeover talks; CrowdStrike down 6% to 8% after hours.
Take-Two Interactive: 'Grand Theft Auto VI' generated $3.79 billion in first-day sales, a record for any entertainment launch according to the company.

blocks.text: Oil

Oil rose Friday but posted a third straight weekly decline. WTI crude settled at $83.98 a barrel, up about 0.9% on the day and down 5.2% for the week; Brent settled at $92.57, up about 0.6% and down 3.4% for the week. Prices got a lift from a tanker incident near the Strait of Hormuz, while expectations of ample global supply have weighed on oil for weeks.
Gold

Gold fell about 3% to 4% Friday to around $3,515-$3,540 an ounce, its lowest since September 2025, according to Kitco and other data providers. Gold has struggled because rising expectations for Fed rate hikes and a strong dollar increase the cost of holding a metal that pays no interest; some investors also sold gold to cover losses elsewhere.
Crypto

Bitcoin, which trades around the clock, was near $58,000 Saturday morning after falling below $56,000 late Friday, its lowest level since July, according to CoinGecko and CoinGlass. Over the past 24 hours it has ranged roughly from $55,100 to $62,200, with more than $2 billion in leveraged positions liquidated, per crypto data sites. CNBC noted bitcoin has been falling alongside stocks rather than acting as a hedge. Ether was near $1,640 in the app's latest quote, holding up better than bitcoin over the past day.
It is Saturday, so there are no US economic releases and stock and bond markets are closed. Crypto trades continuously, and US stock futures reopen Sunday at 6 p.m. ET.

items: Monday: S&P Global flash manufacturing and services PMIs for November, an early read on business activity.
Tuesday: Conference Board consumer confidence for November.

Wednesday, 8:30 a.m. ET: second estimate of third-quarter GDP and October personal income, spending and PCE inflation. One preview expects headline PCE to rise 0.3% for the month, with the annual rate edging up to 3.8% from 3.6%.

blocks.text: No major companies report this weekend. These are the key reports in the holiday-shortened week; some calendars list slightly different dates for Dell, HP and Best Buy, so confirm before trading.

rows: Holiday-season outlook and consumer electronics demand; consensus about $1.49 a share on $9.9 billion revenue
Industrial and auto chip demand amid the chip selloff; consensus about $3.88 a share
AI server orders and backlog; consensus about $6.61 a share on $49.3 billion revenue
PC demand and memory cost pressures; consensus about $0.75 a share
Software spending and AI's effect on business-software demand

blocks.text: Next week is short: US stock markets close Thursday for Thanksgiving and shut early, at 1 p.m. ET, on Friday. The key test comes Wednesday morning, when the government releases its updated third-quarter GDP estimate and the October PCE inflation report together, followed by the Fed's Beige Book. A hotter inflation reading would reinforce expectations for a December hike and could revive talk of a half-point move, while a softer one could ease pressure on bonds and stocks. On the corporate side, Dell's results Tuesday will be closely read for signs of whether AI server demand is holding up after this week's chip rout. Trading volume tends to be light around Thanksgiving, which can amplify price swings when volatility is already high. Black Friday also kicks off the holiday shopping season, a gauge of consumer spending.

bottom_line: Markets head into the weekend in risk-off mode: the S&P 500 and Dow are in correction, chip stocks just had their worst week in decades by some measures, and investors are buying Treasurys and the yen even as the Fed signals another hike. Wednesday's inflation and GDP data are the main scheduled event before the holiday.
